sources.news_title: New York Archdiocese reaches $800 million sexual abuse settlement
sources.text:
The Archdiocese of New York and around 1,300 victims who said they were sexually abused by clergy and lay leaders have come to an $800 million settlement of their legal claims.
Archbishop Ronald Hicks sent an email on Saturday letting clergy know about the settlement of claims under the Child Victims Act. He said the deal would not be finalized until the plaintiffs, their attorneys and archdiocese representatives signed the settlement, a step that is scheduled for next month.
“We are on the verge of being able to, please God, bring some measure of healing and reconciliation to all victim-survivors. This agreement will also allow the archdiocese to turn its full attention once again to its mission of preaching the Gospel, healing the sick, caring for the poor and needy, welcoming the stranger, and educating our children,” Hicks wrote.
According to multiple reports, the settlement is the second-largest involving a Catholic archdiocese in the United States. The National Catholic Reporter wrote that the only larger settlement over sexual abuse claims in the country was by the Archdiocese of Los Angeles, which agreed in 2024 to pay $880 million to 1,000 abuse victims, in addition to $740 million in claims it had paid previously.
“The unanimous agreement of survivors who filed claims against the Archdiocese of New York marks a powerful moment in the pursuit of justice,” Jeff Anderson, an attorney representing people who filed more than 1,000 claims against the Catholic Church in New York, said in a statement appearing in the National Catholic Reporter.
The New York Times, which first published the report, wrote that the settlement would call for each plaintiff to have the option of receiving a lump sum of at least $250,000, or a potentially larger payout after a review of the extent of the abuse each plaintiff has claimed, per the plaintiffs’ lawyers.
New York passed the Child Victims Act in 2019 that extended the deadline for victims of child sexual abuse to bring civil lawsuits until they turn 55 years old. It also temporarily allowed victims to pursue previously time-barred claims.
The Archdiocese of New York includes Manhattan, the Bronx, Staten Island and some Hudson Valley communities.
The settlement announced this weekend follows an agreement reached in May that required approval from everyone who filed a claim.

sources.news_title: New York's archdiocese, survivors of clergy abuse agree to $800M settlement

The Archdiocese of New York and attorneys for about 1,300 parishioners who said they were sexually abused by clergy have agreed to an $800 million settlement of their legal claims, the second-largest involving a Catholic archdiocese in the U.S.
Archbishop Ronald Hicks sent an email Saturday to clergy confirming the settlement after attorneys for the survivors of alleged abuse announced it. Hicks said the agreement will not be final until the parties sign it, an action scheduled for the week of Nov. 6.
The only larger settlement over sexual abuse claims in the U.S. was by the Archdiocese of Los Angeles, which agreed in 2024 to pay $880 million to 1,000 abuse victims, in addition to $740 million in claims it had paid previously. In June, the Archdiocese of San Francisco agreed to a $395 million settlement over about 500 lawsuits filed over clergy abuse, and in December 2025, a federal judge approved a settlement in which the Archdiocese of New Orleans agreed to pay at least $230 million to abuse victims.
The agreement with the New York archdiocese would end more than seven years of lawsuits. The parties agreed to a framework for an agreement in May that required everyone who filed a claim to sign off.
“The unanimous agreement of survivors who filed claims against the Archdiocese of New York marks a powerful moment in the pursuit of justice,” Jeff Anderson, an attorney representing people who filed more than 1,000 of claims against the Catholic Church in New York state, said in a statement. “Through their courage, sacrifice, and determination, survivors have helped bring about a reckoning and a meaningful step toward accountability.”
The Archiocese of New York covers the city's boroughs of the Bronx, Manhattan and Staten Island as well as seven counties to the north of New York City and is home to about 300 churches, more than 150 parochial schools and 2.5 million Catholics.
In his email to clergy, Hicks said that if church members ask about the settlement, “please let them know that much progress has been made.”
“We are on the verge of being able to, please God, bring some measure of healing and reconciliation to all victim-survivors,” he wrote. “This agreement will also allow the archdiocese to turn its full attention once again to its mission of preaching the Gospel, healing the sick, caring for the poor and needy, welcoming the stranger, and educating our children.”
A New York law enacted in 2019 allows survivors of child sexual abuse to file lawsuits against their abusers and institutions that shielded them until they turn 55. “This is an extraordinary achievement for the survivors,” said Trusha Goffe, an attorney in Anderson’s firm. "The survivors remined resolute through years of litigation to reach this monumental settlement.”

sources.news_title: In 2019, New York changed the law to let survivors pursue decades-old abuse claims; seven years later, about 1,300 people have agreed to an $800 million settlement with the Catholic archdiocese, pending signatures
sources.text:
The Catholic Archdiocese of New York has agreed to pay $800 million (£615 million) to around 1,300 survivors who reported sexual abuse by clergy and other church staff. The settlement brings years of legal disputes and negotiations closer to an end. Lawyers representing the survivors announced the agreement. It covers a large number of civil lawsuits filed under a New York state law that temporarily allowed people to bring claims over historical sexual abuse, even when the usual time limit for legal action had passed. Both sides have agreed to the main terms of the financial settlement. However, lawyers said the final documents still need to be processed and formally signed before payments can be made to individual survivors.
Legal changes opened path to justice
The legal action began to grow in 2019, when New York lawmakers passed the Child Victims Act. The law created a temporary period during which adults who had experienced sexual abuse as children could file civil lawsuits, even if the alleged abuse had happened decades earlier. Before the law changed, strict time limits had stopped many people from taking legal action against religious institutions, schools and youth organisations.
 The temporary window led to thousands of lawsuits across New York State against Catholic dioceses, including the Archdiocese of New York. The archdiocese covers Manhattan, the Bronx, Staten Island and seven nearby counties. The large number of claims created financial and legal pressure for several dioceses. Some other Catholic dioceses in New York sought protection from creditors through federal bankruptcy proceedings. The Archdiocese of New York, based in Manhattan, instead tried to settle the claims without entering formal Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings.
Distribution and oversight mechanisms
The $800 million settlement was put together using money from archdiocesan assets, contributions from affiliated religious orders and insurance payments. Under the agreement reached by the lawyers, each survivor's payment will be decided through an independent review process. Administrators will consider the seriousness of the reported abuse, its long-term emotional and physical effects, and the historical records available to support each claim. Lawyers representing the survivors said the amounts would differ among the 1,300 claimants. The money is intended to help cover medical costs, psychological counselling and damages linked to the abuse. The agreement also includes steps aimed at improving transparency. The archdiocese agreed to release more internal records about clergy members who have been credibly accused of abuse. It also agreed to keep public records updated, with the aim of helping prevent similar cases from being hidden in the future.
Impact on local church operations
The settlement will be funded through church reserves, property transactions and insurance payments. The $800 million payout is among the largest single financial settlements agreed by a Catholic jurisdiction in United States history. Cardinal Timothy Dolan, the Archbishop of New York, has previously recognised the serious harm caused by historical abuse within the Church. He described the offences as a dark period in the institution's history and pledged to co-operate with oversight measures. The agreement is expected to help the archdiocese resolve hundreds of pending cases in New York state courts. Many of these lawsuits had remained open since the Child Victims Act took effect in 2019. Representatives for the survivors said that no amount of money could erase the trauma they had experienced. However, they said the settlement offered financial support and a measure of accountability for people who had waited years for their cases to be addressed, including those now reaching older age. The agreement still requires final signatures and the completion of court approval procedures. These steps are expected to be completed over the coming months, after which payments can be arranged for individual claimants.

New York Archdiocese To Name Accused Priests and Open Internal Files Under $800M Sexual Abuse Settlement
The reported agreement would provide compensation while requiring the Church to publish and update names linked to substantiated abuse allegations
The Archdiocese of New York is nearing an $800 million (approximately £630 million) sexual abuse settlement that would not only compensate around 1,300 survivors but also require the Church to publicly identify clergy members and lay leaders credibly accused of abuse, according to a report from the New York Times.
The agreement represents a significant development for survivors who have spent years pursuing claims against the Catholic institution. Beyond financial compensation, the proposed terms include publishing the names of credibly accused individuals on the archdiocese's website and updating the list when future allegations are substantiated.
According to the New York Times, lawyers representing the plaintiffs said they had finalised the settlement and that all 1,300 claimants had agreed to the revised terms. However, an archdiocese spokesperson said on Friday that the parties were still working to complete the agreement.
Public Naming of Accused Clergy at Heart of Deal
One of the most consequential provisions of the proposed settlement is the requirement for the archdiocese to publish the names of clergy members and lay leaders who were credibly accused of sexual abuse.
The list would also have to be updated as future claims were substantiated, according to The New York Times. Survivors and their lawyers said the disclosure requirements could help expose past abuse and support efforts to prevent further harm.
The public release of names could provide greater visibility into allegations that survivors have pursued through years of legal proceedings. It would also create an ongoing disclosure obligation rather than limiting the information released to the settlement itself.
The agreement's reported provisions do not establish that every person named has been criminally convicted. The distinction between a credible accusation and a criminal conviction remains important when reporting allegations of abuse.
The proposed settlement also raises questions about what information the archdiocese would have disclosed if it had instead filed for bankruptcy. According to The New York Times, it remains unclear what disclosures, if any, would have been required under that alternative process.
Survivors Offered Choice on Payouts After Long Legal Fight
The settlement would cover claims from approximately 1,300 people who said they were sexually abused by clergy members and lay leaders. The proposed terms would allow each plaintiff to choose between a lump-sum payment of at least $250,000 (approximately £200,000) or a potentially larger amount determined through a review of the abuse described in their claim.
The arrangement follows years of negotiations, with some survivors initially resisting the proposal because they believed it did not adequately address the harm they experienced.
According to the New York Times, plaintiffs' lawyers said the archdiocese negotiated with one of its insurers to increase the amount available to a small group of holdouts. A separate pool of $20 million (approximately £16 million) would be divided among those claimants.
The lawyers had warned that failing to reach an agreement could lead the archdiocese to file for bankruptcy, potentially reducing payouts and extending litigation that had already lasted years.
Attorney Paul Mones, whose firm represents 33 plaintiffs, praised the survivors for their persistence throughout the negotiations. He said the agreement could provide them with some measure of comfort and healing after years of pain.
Trusha Goffe, an attorney with Jeff Anderson & Associates, also informed clients that the revised agreement had been finalised from the plaintiffs' side. She said further details about the settlement process would follow.
Settlement Follows Wave of Major Catholic Abuse Payouts
The proposed agreement follows other major settlements involving Catholic institutions accused of failing to prevent or address sexual abuse.
According to the New York Times, the Archdiocese of San Francisco agreed in June to pay $395 million (approximately £310 million) to settle claims from more than 530 people who said they had been abused by clergy members and lay leaders. In 2024, the Archdiocese of Los Angeles reached a settlement worth more than $1 billion (approximately £790 million) involving similar claims.
The New York Archdiocese covers Manhattan, the Bronx, Staten Island and several communities in the Hudson Valley.
While the financial terms are substantial, the proposed agreement's public disclosure provisions could have lasting significance for survivors seeking recognition and greater transparency. The requirement to identify credibly accused clergy and lay leaders would make the settlement more than a compensation arrangement.
The agreement's final implementation remains subject to completion of the settlement process. If carried out as described, it would provide compensation to survivors while requiring the archdiocese to make information about substantiated abuse allegations publicly accessible.

Catholic Church agrees to pay $800m to 1,300 sexual abuse victims in New York
The Archdiocese of New York has agreed to pay more than $800 million to hundreds of people who suffered sexual abuse by Catholic clergy, bringing years of negotiations towards a close.
The archdiocese announced the settlement on Saturday, saying the agreement would be formally signed in early November.
New York Archbishop Ronald Hicks disclosed the development in an email to priests, which was later forwarded to journalists by the archdiocese.
“We are on the verge of being able to, please God, bring some measure of healing and reconciliation to all victim-survivors,” Hicks wrote.

The scandals have forced dioceses across the country to pay hundreds of millions of dollars in compensation, with some establishing settlement programmes to resolve victims’ claims without lengthy court proceedings.

New York Archdiocese agrees to $800 million settlement over 1,300 sex abuse claims
The Archdiocese of New York has agreed to an $800 million settlement with approximately 1,300 clergy abuse survivors. The second-largest US Catholic archdiocese payout could advance accountability, healing and further compensation claims.
The Archdiocese of New York has agreed to an $800 million settlement with approximately 1,300 people who said they were sexually abused by clergy, marking the second-largest settlement involving a Catholic archdiocese in the United States.
Lawyers representing the survivors announced the agreement on Saturday, while Archbishop Ronald Hicks confirmed the development in an email to clergy.
The settlement was agreed upon in May, following more than seven years of litigation over claims of sexual abuse.
The agreement will not become final until the parties sign the settlement documents, a step scheduled for the week of November 6, Hicks said.
Jeff Anderson, an attorney representing survivors who filed claims against the Catholic Church in New York, described the unanimous agreement as “a powerful moment in the pursuit of justice”.
He said the survivors' determination had helped bring about greater accountability.
SECOND-LARGEST SETTLEMENT IN US
The $800 million settlement is the second-largest payout involving a Catholic archdiocese in the US. The Archdiocese of Los Angeles agreed in 2024 to pay $880 million to approximately 1,000 survivors of sexual abuse.
The Los Angeles archdiocese had also previously paid $740 million in claims.
In June, the Archdiocese of San Francisco agreed to a $395 million settlement covering approximately 500 lawsuits involving clergy sexual abuse.
In December 2025, a federal judge approved a settlement under which the Archdiocese of New Orleans agreed to pay at least $230 million to survivors.
The Catholic Church has paid billions of dollars in settlements across the US in recent years as survivors have pursued legal action over abuse that occurred decades ago.
The New York agreement also includes the release of documents relating to sexual offenders within the Church. It allows survivors to pursue additional compensation through litigation against the Church's insurers, while avoiding bankruptcy proceedings for the archdiocese.
NEW YORK LAW ENABLED LAWSUITS OVER DECADES-OLD ABUSE
The settlement follows a 2019 New York law that expanded the ability of survivors of child sexual abuse to bring civil lawsuits against their abusers and institutions accused of shielding them.
The law allowed survivors to file claims until the age of 55, while people who were already older than 55 when it was enacted received an additional window to file lawsuits. That period ended in August 2021.
The legislation enabled thousands of people to seek legal recourse over abuse that had occurred years or decades earlier.
Trusha Goffe, an attorney with Anderson's firm, called the agreement an extraordinary achievement for the survivors, saying they had remained determined through years of litigation.
ARCHDIOCESE SAYS SETTLEMENT COULD HELP SURVIVORS HEAL
The Archdiocese of New York serves the city's Bronx, Manhattan and Staten Island boroughs, along with seven counties north of New York City.
It is home to approximately 2.5 million Catholics and operates around 300 churches and more than 150 parochial schools.
In his message to clergy, Hicks said the settlement could help survivors move towards healing and reconciliation.
He also said the agreement would allow the archdiocese to refocus on its religious and charitable responsibilities, including caring for the poor, educating children and serving local communities.

sources.text:
NEW YORK, Oct 25 — The Archdiocese of New York said Saturday it had agreed to a settlement in which the church would pay more than US$800 million (RM3.3 billion) to hundreds of victims of sexual abuse by clergy.
The agreement, to be formally signed in early November, marks the end of years of negotiations with lawyers representing the plaintiffs, as the American Catholic Church has been mired in sexual abuse scandals since the early 2000s.
“We are on the verge of being able to, please God, bring some measure of healing and reconciliation to all victim-survivors,” New York Archbishop Ronald Hicks wrote in an email sent to his priests and forwarded to AFP by the archdiocese.
According to The New York Times, which broke the story, each of the approximately 1,300 victims will receive at least US$250,000, and potentially more depending on the severity of the abuse suffered.
The Archdiocese of New York, which covers Manhattan, Staten Island, the Bronx and several counties north of the city, will now be able to “turn its full attention once again to its mission of preaching the Gospel, healing the sick, caring for the poor and needy, welcoming the stranger, and educating our children,” Hicks’ email said.
Hicks was appointed bishop last year by Pope Leo XIV, replacing the influential conservative Cardinal Timothy Dolan. Before his departure, Dolan had announced the creation of a US$300 million fund to compensate sexual abuse victims.
In the 2000s, press investigations revealed that Catholic priests in the United States had committed sexual abuse against thousands of children over several decades, and that church leaders had often covered up these cases or transferred the offending priests instead of reporting them to civil authorities.
Dioceses across the country have had to pay hundreds of millions of dollars in damages, and programs have been created to compensate victims without going to trial.
Last June, the Archdiocese of San Francisco announced it had reached an agreement to pay US$395 million to about 530 victims of sexual abuse committed by its clergy in order to settle their lawsuits. — AFP

More Than 800 Million Dollars to Resolve Claims From 1,300 Survivors of Clergy and Lay Leader Abuse
NEW YORK, Oct. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Herman Law, representing approximately 260 survivors of sexual abuse by clergy members and lay leaders of the Archdiocese of New York, the second largest group of plaintiffs in the case, announced today that a settlement has been reached resolving claims brought by more than 1,300 survivors against the Archdiocese.
Under the terms of the agreement, each survivor will have the option to receive a lump sum payment of at least 250,000 dollars or pursue a potentially larger payout following an individual review of the abuse they suffered. The settlement, valued at more than 800 million dollars, will be formally signed by the plaintiffs, their counsel, and representatives of the Archdiocese in early November.
The agreement also requires the Archdiocese to publish, and keep updated, a public list of clergy members and lay leaders who have been credibly accused of sexual abuse.

The Archdiocese is now required to publish the names of its abusers and keep that list current. That protects children going forward, and it is long overdue."
The settlement is among the largest reached by a Catholic institution in the United States, following similar agreements by the Archdiocese of San Francisco and the Archdiocese of Los Angeles in recent years.
"This is one of the largest abuse settlements in the history of the Catholic Church in America," Herman said. "It sends a clear message to every diocese still hiding behind bankruptcy and secrecy. For our clients, this is closure. It is justice, vindication, and validation that is long overdue."

The Roman Catholic archdiocese might now avoid bankruptcy by reaching a settlement with 1,300 people who said they had been abused by clergy members and lay leaders.
The Archdiocese of New York and plaintiffs’ lawyers were closing in on a settlement on Friday in which the church would pay more than $800 million to settle claims from 1,300 people who said they had been sexually abused by its clergy members and lay leaders.

But Joseph Zwilling, a spokesman for the archdiocese, said in an interview on Friday night that the parties were still working to finalize the agreement. “We are not quite there yet,” he said.
Terms of the settlement would call for each plaintiff to have the option of receiving a lump-sum payment of at least $250,000, or a potentially larger payout after a review of the extent of the abuse each plaintiff has claimed, according to the plaintiffs’ lawyers.

Progress was also stymied by the deaths of some plaintiffs.
“Tonight, we were able to finalize the settlement with the Archdiocese,” Trusha Goffe, an attorney with Jeff Anderson & Associates, wrote Friday in an email to the firm’s nearly 300 clients who say they were abused. “All of the survivors agreed to the revised deal. This means that the settlement you agreed to will move forward.”
Lawyers for the plaintiffs said they had repeatedly warned their clients that if they did not accept the proposal, the archdiocese would most likely declare bankruptcy, reducing the size of any eventual payout and extending the length of the already yearslong litigation.
To appease the handful of plaintiffs who were resistant to the proposal, the lawyers said, the archdiocese negotiated with one of its insurers to increase the amount of money it would pay the holdouts. They would now receive a pot of $20 million to be evenly distributed among them — an uncommon arrangement that hinged largely on the availability of insurance funds.

In June, the Archdiocese of San Francisco agreed to pay $395 million to settle claims from more than 530 people who said clergy members and lay leaders had abused them. In 2024, the Archdiocese of Los Angeles settled similar claims for more than $1 billion — one of the largest sexual abuse settlements in church history.
